questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point
questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}+x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+x) \\  & =2x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,2):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=2(1)+1=3
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}$ at the point $(1,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-4{x}^{5/2}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{2}-10(1)^{3/2}=-7\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line  ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{7}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{2}-5$ at the point $(2,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}-5.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-5)=2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(2)=2(2)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2}-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{1/2}-4(1)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=1.
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x$ at the point $(1,9).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-5}+7x) \\  & =-10{x}^{-6}+7.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=-10(1)^{-6}+7=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt[3]{x}$ at the point $(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{4}).$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt[3]{x}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{2}\sqrt[3]{x}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{4}):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{1}{8})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{2}}}=2
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{3}{4} & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-\frac{1}{8}) \\ 16(y-\frac{3}{4}) & =16\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (x-\frac{1}{8}) \\ 16y-12 & =-8(x-\frac{1}{8}) \\ 16y-12 & =-8x+1 \\ 8x+16\cdot y & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{8}{x}^{6}-\frac{7}{4}{x}^{3}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{8}{x}^{6}-\frac{7}{4}{x}^{3})=\frac{3}{4}{x}^{5}-\frac{21}{4}{x}^{2}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,-6):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(2)=\frac{3}{4}({2}^{5})-\frac{21}{4}({2}^{2})=3
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-6) & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (x-2) \\ -3(y+6) & =x-2 \\ -3y-18 & =x-2 \\ x+3\cdot y & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=3{x}^{2}+4x$ at the point $(1,7)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=3{x}^{2}+4x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+4x)=6x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,7):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=6(1)+4=10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(7) & =-\frac{1}{10}(x-1) \\ 10y-70 & =-x+1 \\ x+10y & =71.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p+q=10+71=81.$

questions.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x$ at the point $(1,3)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p-q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-2}-x) \\  & =-8{x}^{-3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-8(1)^{-3}-1=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3) & =\frac{1}{9}(x-1) \\ 9y-27 & =x-1 \\ x-9y & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p-q=-9-(-26)=17.$

Let $f(x)=6{x}^{2}-7x+4.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{2}-7x+4)=12x-7
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(0,4):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(0)=12(0)-7=-7
$$

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{7}.

questions.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}$ at the point $(8,12)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/3} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(8)=\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{8}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-12 & =-(x-8) \\ y & =-x+8+12 \\ y & =20-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =20-0 \\ y & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,20).$

questions.problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=4-{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-{x}^{2})=-2x.
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=-2(1)=-2,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}+3 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =-\frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,-5,0\,).$

questions.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+2 \\ y & =-x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0+3 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,3).$

questions.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2} \\  & =3\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=3\sqrt{1}=3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{1}{3}+2 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at  $(7,0).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac 1 4.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$
